name: Aare at Klingnau
stretch: Döttingen to the mouth of the Aare in the Rhine
summary: Aargau first put the wild lower Aare between dams, and in 1931–1935 a power station dammed it into the Klingnau reservoir.
why: Near its mouth the Aare once moved freely across a wide valley floor. It made many arms, gravel islands, reed beds and floodplain forests. After heavy rain the water rose fast, partly because many forests in the catchment had been cut in the 19th century. Floods did a lot of damage.

From 1886 the canton of Aargau put the river step by step into a channel between dams. Behind the dams the old floodplains became dry. Then a power company built the Klingnau power station (1931–1935). It raised the Aare by 6.1 m and made a lake (a reservoir) about 3 km long.

The slow water in the reservoir dropped huge amounts of fine mud. Shallow water and mud banks grew, and reeds and willows grew on them. Today the reservoir is a bird reserve of international importance, but the natural movement of the river is mostly gone.

stops.title: A wide, free river
text: In 1884 the Aare between Döttingen and Koblenz was a wide river with many arms. The red line shows the main channel. The red area shows the wide bed with gravel islands and side arms.
Floods often covered the low land. Few people lived on the valley floor.

stops.title: Dams and a reservoir
text: From 1886 the river was put between dams, step by step. From 1931 to 1935 the Klingnau power station was built at the lower end. The water rose by 6.1 m behind the weir (a low dam in a river).
The blue area is the reservoir. The red line shows where the main channel was before. Most of the old islands are now under water or under mud.

stops.title: A bird reserve
text: Today mud and reeds fill much of the reservoir. The blue line is the Aare today, the red line the old channel of 1884.
The shallow water is a resting place for thousands of water birds. In some old side arms the canton has dug out the mud again, so that floodplain plants and animals can live there.

name: Aare canal at Gösgen
summary: A weir at Winznau sends most of the Aare into a straight canal of about 5 km to the Gösgen power station; the old loop of the river gets only a little water.
why: Below Olten the Aare made a wide loop to the south, past Schachen and Däniken. In the early 20th century Switzerland built many river power stations to make electricity for industry and railways. The fall of the Aare between Olten and Niedergösgen was useful for this.
From 1913 to 1917 a canal was dug from a weir at Winznau to a power station at Niedergösgen. The station started in November 1917. The canal cuts off the loop. It is about 4.8 km long.

Since then most of the water flows through the canal. The old loop ("Alte Aare") gets only the water that the weir lets through. The power station was renewed in 1997–2000. People now discuss how much water the old Aare must get, for fish and for the floodplain.

stops.title: The loop of the Aare
text: In 1910 all the water of the Aare flowed through a big loop south of Obergösgen. The red line shows this loop.
Rafts with wood and goods still used the river in the 19th century. Obergösgen was a place where rafters loaded and unloaded.

lines.name: Aare before the canal, loop past Schachen (map of 1910)

stops.title: A straight canal
text: From 1913 to 1917 workers dug a canal (a river bed dug by people) from the weir at Winznau to the power station at Niedergösgen. The blue line shows it. It is about 4.8 km long.
The weir holds the Aare back and sends most of the water into the canal. The old loop (red) became a quiet river with little water.

lines.name: Aare before the canal, loop past Schachen (map of 1910)
Power station canal Winznau–Niedergösgen (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: Two rivers side by side
text: Today the canal (blue) and the old loop (red) still run side by side. Houses and factories now stand between them.
The power station was completely renewed in 1997–2000. It makes about 12% more electricity from the same water.

lines.name: Aare before the canal, loop past Schachen (map of 1910)
Power station canal Winznau–Niedergösgen (OpenStreetMap)

notes: HLS (Obergösgen) gives 1913–1917 for the canal; Alpiq gives 4.8 km; SRF gives November 1917 and the 1997–2000 renewal. The old loop was traced on the map of 1910; the part of the old loop that is still a river today was not traced separately. Place markers are approximate.

name: Aare between Wildegg and Brugg
summary: For the Wildegg–Brugg power station the Aare was dammed at Schinznach Bad and most of its water was sent into a concrete canal to Brugg.
why: Between Wildegg and Brugg the Aare flowed in a natural bed with many arms. In floods the bed was up to 500 m wide, and the arms changed again and again. The valley floor near Villnachern was gravel, islands and floodplain forest.

After the Second World War Switzerland needed more electricity. From 1949 to 1953 the Wildegg–Brugg power station was built. It is the largest power station on the Aare. A weir at Schinznach Bad holds the river back, and a canal takes most of the water to the power house near Brugg. The HLS says the work brought "great changes to the landscape".

The old river bed (the "Alte Aare") now gets only a part of the water. In the last 20 years the canton of Aargau has made new side arms and gravel areas there, as part of its floodplain park (Auenschutzpark).

stops.title: Arms, islands and gravel
text: In 1950 the Aare near Villnachern still had a wide bed with arms and islands (red area). The red line shows the main channel.
Floods moved the gravel and changed the arms. Pine and willow forests grew on the islands.

name: Limmat (Zurich to Dietikon)
stretch: Zurich-Altstetten to Oetwil an der Limmat
summary: After the floods of 1874 and 1876 the canton of Zurich cut the loops of the Limmat below Zurich and put the river between dams.
why: Below Zurich the Limmat made loops through wet meadows and floodplain forest. Each village built its own bank defences, often to push the water to the other bank. Floods damaged fields and roads, for example in 1846, 1874 and 1876. In June 1876 about a third of a normal year's rain fell in Zurich in six days.

Only three months after this flood, on 23 October 1876, the people of Zurich accepted a new water law. The canton now had to correct the large rivers (Rhine, Töss, Thur, Glatt, Limmat, Sihl), and paid with loans, money from the communes and a federal subsidy. The canton engineer Kaspar Wetli led the work.

On the Limmat the work started in 1880 with a cut at Schönenwerd. More cuts followed near Engstringen, Oetwil and Dietikon until 1896, and the old bed at Dietikon was filled. After a flood in 1910 the dams were raised in 1912. Because land was expensive, the canton left almost no flat land between river and dams. Today only small parts of the old floodplain are left.

stops.title: Loops below Zurich
text: The red line shows the Limmat in 1885. It made loops near Glanzenberg and Dietikon and had several arms around islands.
In 1880 the first cut (a short new channel through a bend) was dug at Schönenwerd. Most of the loops were still there.

lines.name: Limmat before the correction, with its loops (map of 1885)

stops.title: Cuts and dams
text: From 1884 to 1896 workers dug cuts near Engstringen, Oetwil and the mouth of the Reppisch. The blue line shows the new, smoother bed. In 1896 the old bed at Dietikon was filled.
Dams of earth with stone blocks on the river side now kept the water in its bed. Only Swiss workers could be employed, so the work also helped people without jobs.

Limmat today, in its corrected bed (swisstopo swissTLM3D)

stops.title: A city river
text: Today the Limmat flows in the bed of the correction (blue). Houses, roads and railways now stand on the old floodplain (red).
Near Kloster Fahr and Dietikon small parts of the old floodplain forest are protected.

name: Lorze (Baar plain)
summary: In the 1970s the Lorze got a new, shorter bed from Baar straight to Lake Zug near the town of Zug; part of the old bed became the motorway.
why: The Lorze is the main river of the canton of Zug. Below Baar it flowed west across the flat Baar plain and reached Lake Zug between Zug and Cham. In floods, for example in 1861, 1910 and 1934, it covered the low land.

In the 19th and 20th centuries people built canals and dams along the Lorze, for water power and against floods. In the 1970s the canton gave the river a new bed from Baar south-west to the lake. At the same time the motorway N4a was built, and part of the old river bed was used for it.

Even earlier, in 1591–1592, the town of Zug had deepened the outlet of the lake (also the Lorze) at Cham. This lowered Lake Zug by about 2 m. That work happened long before the first maps of this series.

stops.title: Across the Baar plain
text: The red line shows the Lorze in 1960. From Baar it flowed west across the plain, past Steinhausen, and reached the lake east of Cham.
Floods in 1861, 1910 and 1934 covered parts of the plain.

lines.name: Old course of the Lorze through the Baar plain (map of 1960)

stops.title: A new bed to the lake
text: In the 1970s the Lorze got a new bed (blue). It runs from Baar straight to Lake Zug, north of the town of Zug.
A part of the old bed (red) was used for the new motorway. Around it the plain filled with roads, houses and businesses.

Lorze today, in its new bed of the 1970s (swisstopo swissTLM3D)

stops.title: Lorze today
text: Today the Lorze flows in the bed of the 1970s (blue). The red line shows the old course.
The new mouth near Zug made the river shorter and the flood risk for the plain smaller.

The 1591–1592 lowering is from HLS and BAFU. The old course was traced on the map of 1960; the new line is clipped west of Baar.

name: Sihl (Sihlsee reservoir)
stretch: Sihl valley between Euthal and the dam north of Einsiedeln
summary: The Sihl was dammed north of Einsiedeln; the reservoir drowned a high valley of farms and moors to make electricity for the railways.
why: Near Einsiedeln the Sihl wound through a wide, flat high valley with moors, meadows and many farms. Since 1897 the canton of Schwyz, the district of Einsiedeln and the cantons of Zurich and Zug talked about a reservoir there. They argued about payments, cheap electricity, new roads and compensation for the farmers.

From 1932 to 1937 the Etzelwerk company, owned by the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) and the NOK power company, built the dam. Its supporters spoke of new jobs and of Swiss self-supply with electricity. The water goes to a power station at Altendorf on Lake Zurich and makes electricity for the railways.

The lake covered 943 ha of good farmland. According to the HLS, 452 farm businesses were affected. Only part of the families got a new farm near the lake. The reservoir also changed the Sihl below it: it takes away water, but it also reduces flood peaks.

stops.title: A high valley with farms
text: In 1930 the Sihl (red line) meandered through a flat valley with moors and meadows. Farms and small villages such as Willerzell and Euthal stood on the valley floor.
The blue area shows the lake that would later cover this valley.

lines.name: Sihl before the reservoir (map of 1930)

stops.title: The valley under water
text: From 1932 to 1937 a dam was built north of the valley. The water rose and filled the valley (blue). The red line shows the river under the lake.
New roads and two viaducts (long bridges) were built across the lake. Many families had to leave their farms.

lines.name: Sihl before the reservoir (map of 1930)

stops.title: Sihlsee today
text: Today the Sihlsee is about 8.5 km long and covers 11 km². The red line shows the old Sihl under the water.
The reservoir holds back flood water. But below the dam the Sihl now carries less water than before.

lines.name: Sihl before the reservoir (map of 1930)

notes: Facts from HLS (Sihlsee, Sihl). The National Museum blog says about a third of the families were rehoused; the text says only "part". The old river was traced semi-automatically on the map of 1930; small loops are simplified.

name: Wägitaler Aa (Wägitalersee)
summary: A dam on the Wägitaler Aa made a reservoir for electricity in 1924; the old village of Innerthal went under water.
why: In the upper Wägital the Aa flowed through a flat valley floor with the village of Innerthal, a church, farms and a small spa. People had discussed a power station here since the late 19th century. In 1909 the city of Zurich bought the spa hotel, also to secure the water.

Electricity use in Switzerland grew fast. A dam was finished in 1924, and the water began to fill the valley in July 1924. The church of the old village was blown up in August 1924. The water drives the Rempen power station lower down the valley, mostly in winter.

The planned resettlement was only partly done. Sixteen new houses were built on the slope, and a new church and school above the lake. More than 100 people left the commune. Innerthal had 363 people in 1900 and only 223 in 1930.

stops.title: A village on the valley floor
text: In 1920 the Aa (red line) flowed through a flat valley. The village of Innerthal stood on the valley floor.
The blue area shows the lake that would soon cover it.

lines.name: Wägitaler Aa before the reservoir (map of 1920)

stops.title: The village under water
text: In 1924 the dam was finished. The water rose and covered the river, the fields and the old village (blue).
A new Innerthal was built higher up, on the north-east shore of the lake.

text: Today the lake is about 4 km² large and holds 150 million m³ of water. Most of the water is used for electricity in winter.

name: Lungerersee (lowered and dammed again)
summary: Lungern lowered its lake by 18 m through a tunnel to win farmland (1790–1836); in 1921 a power station dammed the lake again and the new land went back under water.
why: Lungern had little flat land. To win farmland, the commune lowered its lake. From 1790 to 1836 people dug a tunnel of about 420 m through the rock ridge at Kaiserstuhl. The lake fell from about 675 m to 657 m above sea level, and about 170 ha of new land appeared, mostly at the south end near the village.
The new land brought problems. The streams that flow into the lake now had a lower end, so they cut deeper into their beds and damaged the new fields.

In 1921 the lake was dammed again for the Lungerersee power station (owned by the CKW power company, concession 1919). Since then the level moves between 667.5 m and 692 m. At high water the lake is larger than before 1790, and most of the land won in 1836 is under water again.

stops.title: A smaller lake
text: In 1836 the work on the tunnel was finished and the lake was 18 m lower. The red line and area show the small lake as it was until 1921. South of it lay the new land (Seefeld) with meadows and paths.
The blue area shows how large the lake is today.

lines.name: Shore of the lowered lake, 1836–1921 (map of 1920)

areas.name: Lungerersee today, dammed again for electricity (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: Dammed again
text: In 1921 the lake was dammed for a power station. The water rose again by up to 35 m (blue). It covered the land won in 1836.
The lake now stores water for a power station. The red line shows the shore of the lowered lake.

lines.name: Shore of the lowered lake, 1836–1921 (map of 1920)

areas.name: Lungerersee today, dammed again for electricity (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: Lungerersee today
text: Today the lake is about 3.5 km long and holds about 50 million m³ of water. Its level changes by up to 25 m during the year, because the power station uses the water.
The red line shows the shore of the lowered lake of 1836–1921.

The shore of the lowered lake was extracted automatically from the blue lake fill of the map of 1920 and checked by eye. No map of this series shows the lake before 1836.

name: Bünz
summary: In the years after the First World War the canton of Aargau straightened the Bünz from Muri to Othmarsingen and drained the marshes of the valley to grow more food.
why: The valley floor of the Bünz is almost flat. The stream wound through it and often flooded wide areas. Much of the land was marsh or wet meadow, and farmers could only cut litter (straw for the stables) there. People had wanted a correction for almost 50 years.

The First World War showed that Switzerland had to grow more of its own food. In March 1918 the Aargau government wrote that protecting fertile land from floods and turning marsh into fields was now a first duty of the state. Between 1919 and 1942 the Bünz was straightened from Muri to Othmarsingen, and the wet land was drained.

The new bed had a trapezoid shape and banks of stone blocks or concrete. In Othmarsingen it could carry 60 m³/s instead of 20 m³/s. But the stream became a straight, dull channel with little life. The last part, from Möriken to Wildegg, was not corrected because of the cost. There a flood in May 1999 made a new wild floodplain, the Bünzaue, which is now protected.

stops.title: Meanders and marsh
text: In 1915 the Bünz (red line) wound through the valley between Wohlen and Dottikon. The red areas show wet meadows and marsh along it.
Floods covered the valley floor often. Farmers could use much of it only for litter.

stops.title: A straight channel

The map of 1945 shows a grid of new fields where the marsh was. The red line shows the old meanders.

text: Today the Bünz still flows in its straight bed (blue), between fields, roads and villages.
Further north, between Möriken and Wildegg, the stream was never corrected. There the flood of 1999 made a new floodplain with gravel banks and islands.
